As the respondent's application to the Tribunal was out of time, the panel orders that the appeal be allowed, the decision under appeal be set aside, and the Tribunal proceedings be dismissed. (a) the date on which the contractor handed over possession of the work to the owner,
(b) the date on which the contractor last attended the site to carry out work (other than work to remedy any defect that does not affect practical completion),
(c) the date of issue of an occupation certificate under the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979 that authorises commencement of the use or occupation of the work,
(d) (in the case of owner-builder work) the date that is 18 months after the issue of the owner-builder permit for the work.
In our view, in accordance with s 3B(1) of the HB Act, the statutory warranty period commenced on completion of the building works within the meaning of the contract; that is, when the works reached practical completion. If the contract had not provided for when the building works were complete and s 3B(1) was not engaged, then s 3B(2) and s 3B(3) of the HB Act would apply. It is not in dispute that the owners took possession of the works on 13 July 2017. In this case, that would be the relevant date in accordance with s 3B(3)(a) of the Act. Issue of the FOC is not the completion date of the works under s 3B.
Overall, we conclude that the Tribunal erred in finding that the date of completion of the building works was 20 October 2010, when the FOC was issued. In making this finding, the Tribunal misinterpreted the contract and did not correctly apply sections 48K(7) and 3B of the HB Act. Ground 6 is established. In our view, if the completion date was not the date of practical completion (8 July 2010), it was the date on which the works were handed over the owners (13 July 2021).
If we have erred in finding that the Tribunal’s finding in relation to completion date raises a question of law, then for the reasons set out above, we conclude that the Tribunal’s finding in this regard is against the weight of evidence. We would grant leave to appeal on this ground because we consider that the Tribunal’s finding concerning the completion date gives rise to an injustice to the builder which is reasonably clear.
Disposition of the appeal
It follows from our conclusion that the parties did not enter into a new contract or vary their original contract that the respondent’s application to the Tribunal was out of time. This is because the owners’ proceedings were not commenced within seven years of completion of the building works.
The Tribunal has no power to extend time for the making of an application under the HB Act: S & G Homes Pty Ltd t/as Pavilion Homes v Owen [2015] NSWCATAP 190 at [53].

2. **Start small**: If you're not feeling motivated, don't aim for your usual 10,000 steps. Start with a smaller goal, like 5,000 or 7,000 steps, and build up gradually.

7. **Track your progress**: Use your Fitbit app to track your progress and see how close you are to reaching your goal. This can be a great motivator!
8. **Make it enjoyable**: Listen to music, podcasts, or audiobooks while you walk to make the experience more enjoyable.
9. **Get some fresh air**: Take a short walk outside, even if it's just around the block. Natural light and fresh air can help boost your mood and energy levels.
10. **Be kind to yourself**: Remember that it's okay to have off days. Don't be too hard on yourself if you don't reach your goal. Instead, focus on getting moving and doing your best.

[2023-05-27] assistant: Shaping onigiri can take a bit of practice, but with some tips and tricks, you'll be a pro in no time!

**Tips for Shaping Perfect Onigiri:**

1. **Use the right rice:** Japanese short-grain rice is stickier and clingier than regular rice, making it ideal for shaping onigiri. If you're using regular rice, try adding a small amount of rice vinegar to help it hold its shape.
2. **Prepare the rice:** Cool the cooked rice to room temperature. This will help it hold its shape better. If the rice is too hot, it will be too sticky and difficult to shape.
3. **Use the right amount of rice:** Use about 1/2 cup of cooked rice for each onigiri. This will give you a good balance between size and shape.
4. **Moisten your hands:** Dampen your hands with water to prevent the rice from sticking to them.
5. **Shape the onigiri:**
	* Hold a small handful of rice in your palm and gently shape it into a triangle.
	* Apply gentle pressure to the rice, starting from the center and working your way outwards.
	* Use your thumbs to shape the corners and edges of the triangle.
	* Make sure the rice is evenly distributed and the edges are crisp.
6. **Tuck in the filling:** Place your chosen filling (e.g., salmon, tuna, pickled plum) in the center of the triangle and gently fold the rice over it.
7. **Press and shape:** Press the onigiri gently to flatten the bottom and shape the top into a triangle.
8. **Repeat and refine:** Continue shaping and refining the onigiri until you're happy with the shape.

**Common Mistakes to Avoid:**

* Using too much rice, which can make the onigiri too large and difficult to shape.
* Applying too much pressure, which can cause the rice to crack or break.
* Not moistening your hands, which can cause the rice to stick to them.
* Not shaping the onigiri gently, which can cause them to become misshapen.

**Practice Makes Perfect:**
Don't be discouraged if your first few onigiri don't turn out perfectly. With practice, you'll develop the technique and get a feel for the right amount of pressure and shaping required.

I hope these tips help you create beautiful and delicious onigiri!
